1.topic: Building major scales and singing in rounds
1.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. build a major scale on G using the tone and semitone pattern;
2. explain why F must be sharpened in G major;
3. use movable-do solfa on a new starting note;
4. sing a simple round, and learn a long song such as the National Anthem phrase by phrase.

## Materials

A keyboard or a picture of a piano keyboard, a solfa ladder, copies of a simple round, copies of the words of the National Anthem.

## Starter

Sing the C major scale in solfa. Ask: what if we begin on a different note? Will the same pattern still work?

## Development

1. Revise the pattern: tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone.
2. Build the scale on G: G A B C D E F# G. Test each step. E to F natural is only a semitone, but the pattern needs a tone, so F must be raised to F sharp. F# to G is then the semitone.
3. Movable do: the first note of any major scale is called do. In G major, do = G, re = A, mi = B, fa = C, sol = D, la = E, ti = F#.
4. Intervals: do to mi is a third; do to sol is a fifth.
5. Rounds: the same melody begins in groups one after another. Teach the class to keep their own part.
6. Learning a long song: learn the words, then the tune phrase by phrase, then join the phrases.

## Class activity

Learners write the G major scale in letters and solfa, mark the semitones, then sing a short round in three groups.

## Evaluation

1. Which note must be sharpened in G major?
2. If do is G, what is sol?
3. What is a round?

## Assignment

Worksheet on the app. Write the G major scale and mark the semitones.

reading.content:
# Building major scales and singing in rounds

## The pattern works on any note

In JSS 1 you learned the C major scale. A major scale can begin on any note, and it always follows the same pattern:

**tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone**

On the white keys, C major fits this pattern with no sharps or flats. To start on another note, we may have to **sharpen** (raise by a semitone) or **flatten** (lower by a semitone) one note to keep the pattern.

## G major

Start on G and count the steps:

| Step | From | To | Size |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | G | A | tone |
| 2 | A | B | tone |
| 3 | B | C | semitone |
| 4 | C | D | tone |
| 5 | D | E | tone |
| 6 | E | F# | tone |
| 7 | F# | G | semitone |

The natural F is only a semitone above E. The pattern needs a **tone** there, so F is raised to **F sharp (F#)**. The scale of G major is:

**G A B C D E F# G**

The semitones are between **B and C** and between **F# and G**.

## Movable-do solfa

In solfa, do is always the first note of the scale, wherever that note is. In G major:

| do | re | mi | fa | sol | la | ti | do |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| G | A | B | C | D | E | F# | G |

So the tune sung to solfa can be sung in any key.

## Intervals in solfa

- do to mi is a **third**.
- do to sol is a **fifth**.
- do to the upper do is an **octave**.

## Singing in a round

A **round** is a song in which every group sings the same melody but begins one after another. The teacher divides the class into groups. Group 1 starts. Group 2 begins when group 1 reaches the second line, and group 3 when group 2 reaches the second line. Each group keeps to a steady beat and sings its own part without following the others. At the end, the groups finish one after another, or stop together on the teacher's sign.

## Learning a long song

For a long song such as the National Anthem, learn the words, then the tune, **phrase by phrase**, and join the phrases at the end. Breathe at the ends of phrases and finish each line together.

2.topic: Voice range, choir parts, warming up and diction
2.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. explain vocal range and the changing voice;
2. place singers in SATB parts according to their voices;
3. perform a safe vocal warm-up;
4. explain diction and why it matters in singing.

## Materials

A keyboard or the teacher's voice, a list of the class's voices, a marker board.

## Starter

Ask each learner to hum their highest and lowest comfortable notes. Discuss why the class has different ranges.

## Development

1. Range is the span from the lowest to the highest note a singer can sing comfortably.
2. Voice change: in the early teens, boys' voices deepen and may crack; take care not to strain them.
3. Choir parts: soprano, alto, tenor and bass. Place singers by comfortable range, not by height or friendship.
4. Warm-up: relax neck and shoulders, slow deep breaths, gentle humming, easy scales on 'ah'.
5. Diction is clear pronunciation of words in singing. Practise consonants at the ends of words and open vowels.

## Class activity

The class is divided into SATB parts using each learner's range and sings a short hymn with the warm-up first.

## Evaluation

1. What is vocal range?
2. Why do singers warm up?
3. What is diction?

## Assignment

Quiz on the app. Try the warm-up at home and write down your highest and lowest notes.

reading.title: Taking care of a singing voice
reading.content:
# Voice range, choir parts, warm-ups and diction

## Vocal range

A singer's **range** is the span from the lowest to the highest note they can sing comfortably. Two people of the same age can have different ranges. A choir master listens to each singer and places them where the notes fit.

## Changing voices

In the early teens, a boy's voice becomes deeper. This is called the **voice breaking** or the voice changing. The voice may crack or slip between high and low. It is not a problem. Boys going through it should sing in the range they can manage and not force high notes. Girls' voices also deepen slightly, but less.

## SATB parts

A mixed choir has four parts:

- **Soprano:** high female or child voices.
- **Alto:** lower female voices (and some boys).
- **Tenor:** higher male voices.
- **Bass:** lower male voices.

The choir master places singers by **comfortable range**, not by height or friendship. When each part sings its own notes at the same time, the choir makes **harmony**.

## Warming up

Singers warm up before singing, just as footballers warm up before a match, so the voice is ready and does not strain. A simple warm-up:

1. Roll the shoulders and relax the neck.
2. Take slow, deep breaths with the belly moving out.
3. Hum gently, starting low and moving higher.
4. Sing easy scales on "ah", up and down.

## Diction

**Diction** means clear pronunciation of the words in a song. A song with unclear diction cannot be understood by the listener, however beautiful the tune.

Tips for good diction:

- Open the mouth enough for the vowels.
- Pronounce the consonants at the ends of words, such as the t in "night".
- Sing the words as you would say them.
- Learn the meaning of the words, so you sing them with feeling.

## Tone and care

Sing in the voice that is natural to you, not a copy of someone else's. Drink water, rest tired voices and do not shout.

3.topic: Traditional Nigerian music: instruments, styles and their uses
3.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. name traditional instruments of the Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa and say how they are played;
2. group instruments as membranophones, idiophones, aerophones and chordophones;
3. describe the occasions on which traditional music is used;
4. explain call-and-response singing.

## Materials

Recordings or live demonstrations of a talking drum, ogene, udu, kakaki and goge (or pictures), a chart of instrument groups.

## Starter

Play a short clip of a talking drum. Ask what the drum is 'saying' and why people understand it.

## Development

1. Instrument groups: membranophones (stretched skin: drums such as dundun, bata, gangan), idiophones (the body of the instrument vibrates: ogene gong, udu clay pot, sekere gourd rattle, ekwe slit drum), aerophones (air: kakaki long trumpet, algaita, flutes) and chordophones (strings: goge one-string fiddle).
2. Yoruba: dundun and bata drums, sekere. Igbo: ogene, udu, ekwe. Hausa: kakaki, algaita, goge, gangan.
3. Occasions: royal courts, festivals, weddings, funerals, farming, masquerades and storytelling.
4. Features: call and response, repetition, improvisation, and drums that imitate the tones of spoken language.
5. Modern popular styles grew from traditional ones.

## Class activity

Groups sort picture cards of instruments into the four groups and match each to its people. Then the class practises a call-and-response song.

## Evaluation

1. Which group does an udu belong to?
2. Name an aerophone.
3. What is call and response?

## Assignment

Problem set on the app. Find out which traditional instruments are used in your family's hometown.

reading.title: The sounds of home
reading.content:
# Traditional Nigerian music

Nigeria has hundreds of ethnic groups and many traditions of music. Music is part of daily life: it is played when a king is installed, when a baby is named, when a farmer clears the field and when a person is buried.

## Instruments and their groups

Instruments are grouped by how they make their sound.

**Membranophones** make sound from a stretched skin.

- The **dundun**, a Yoruba talking drum, is held under the arm and struck with a curved stick. The drummer squeezes the cords to change the pitch, so the drum can imitate the tones of Yoruba speech.
- The **bata** is a double-headed Yoruba drum.
- The **gangan** is the Hausa talking drum.

**Idiophones** make sound from the body of the instrument itself.

- The **ogene** is an Igbo metal gong, struck with a stick.
- The **udu** is a clay pot with a hole. The player strikes it with the palm to make deep sounds.
- The **sekere** is a gourd covered with a net of beads, shaken or struck against the palm.
- The **ekwe** is a wooden slit drum.

**Aerophones** make sound from moving air.

- The **kakaki** is a very long trumpet blown at the Hausa emir's court to announce him.
- The **algaita** is a Hausa double-reed horn, like an oboe.

**Chordophones** make sound from strings.

- The **goge** is a Hausa one-string fiddle played with a bow.

## Occasions

- **Royal courts:** praise singers recall the history of the ruler and his family.
- **Festivals and weddings:** drumming and dance bring the whole village together.
- **Funerals:** songs of mourning and remembrance.
- **Farming:** work songs keep people in time as they hoe and harvest.
- **Masquerades:** drums and songs call the masks.

## Features of traditional music

**Call and response.** A leader sings a line (the call) and the group answers with a fixed reply. It suits communal events because everyone can join in, even if they do not know all the words, and it keeps workers in the same rhythm.

**Repetition and improvisation.** A short line is repeated while the leader adds new words or phrases.

**Talking drums.** Languages like Yoruba use tone (high, middle, low), so a drum that copies the tones can send messages.

## Today

Highlife, juju, fuji and afrobeats grew out of traditional rhythms and instruments, mixed with new ones. Knowing the old styles helps us understand the new ones.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. name the parts of the recorder and hold it correctly;
2. blow with a gentle, steady breath and tongue each note;
3. play B, A and G with the correct fingers;
4. read B, A and G on the staff and play a simple tune.

## Materials

A recorder for each learner (or one per pair, cleaned between users), a staff on the board with B, A and G, a chart of finger positions.

## Starter

Play a short tune on a recorder. Ask: how do you think a recorder makes its sound? Take answers, then show the mouthpiece and the holes.

## Development

1. Parts: the mouthpiece (beak), the body with seven holes at the front and a thumb hole at the back, and the foot.
2. Holding: left hand on top, right hand below. Left thumb covers the back hole. Cover each hole with the soft pad of the finger so that no air leaks.
3. Breathing: place the beak lightly between the lips, not the teeth. Blow gently and steadily as if saying a soft 'tu'.
4. Fingering: B is the thumb and the first finger of the left hand. A adds the second finger. G adds the third finger.
5. Reading: B is on the middle line of the staff, A in the second space, G on the second line. Practise B A G, then a simple tune.
6. Care: do not blow hard, wipe away moisture, keep it in its bag and clean the mouthpiece before sharing.

## Class activity

Learners play B, A, G slowly four times each, then play 'B A G, B A G, G G G G, A A A A, B A G' from the board, counting the beats.

## Evaluation

1. Which fingers play G?
2. What causes a squeaky sound?
3. Where is B on the staff?

## Assignment

Worksheet on the app. Practise the three notes for five minutes each day and write which note you find hardest.

reading.title: Learning the recorder
reading.content:
# Playing the recorder

## Parts of the recorder

The soprano recorder has three parts: the **mouthpiece** (or beak), the **body**, which has **seven finger holes at the front and a thumb hole at the back**, and the **foot**. It is held in a straight line in front of you, pointing down.

## Holding it

- Left hand at the top, right hand below.
- Left thumb covers the hole at the back.
- Cover the holes with the **soft pads** of the fingers, not the tips. If a hole is not fully covered, air leaks and the note squeaks.

## Breathing and tonguing

- Rest the beak **lightly between the lips**, not between the teeth.
- Blow **gently and steadily**, as though you were saying a quiet "tu" to start each note.
- Blowing hard makes a shrill, squeaky sound and the note goes out of tune.

## The notes B, A and G

All three use the left hand only.

| Note | Fingers |
| --- | --- |
| B | Thumb and first finger |
| A | Thumb, first and second fingers |
| G | Thumb, first, second and third fingers |

To move from B to A, **add** the second finger. To move from A to G, **add** the third finger. The other fingers stay down.

## Reading the notes

On the staff in the treble clef:

- **B** is on the middle (third) line.
- **A** is in the second space from the bottom.
- **G** is on the second line from the bottom.

## A first tune

"B A G, B A G, G G G G, A A A A, B A G" is a simple tune you can play with these three notes. Count the beats: each note is a crotchet, one beat. Where there are two notes in a beat, play them quickly.

## Care of the recorder

1. Do not blow too hard.
2. After playing, shake out and wipe away moisture.
3. Keep it in its bag or case, out of the sun.
4. If it is shared, clean the mouthpiece with a cloth and a little disinfectant first.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. explain how drama began in worship and community celebration;
2. describe the forms of drama: tragedy, comedy, melodrama and farce;
3. name the elements of drama;
4. name the people in a theatre production and say what each does.

## Materials

Pictures of an Egungun masquerade, a Greek theatre and a Nigerian stage production; two short scripts (one funny, one sad) read by learners; a marker board.

Ask two learners to act a short quarrel over a lost pen, with no script. Ask the class: what makes it drama?

1. Drama began as ritual: people acted, danced and sang to honour gods and ancestors, and to tell stories of the community. In Greece, festivals for Dionysus grew into tragedy and comedy. In Nigeria, masquerades such as Egungun, and the Tiv Kwagh-hir with puppets and masks, are traditions of performance.
2. Alarinjo is a Yoruba travelling theatre that grew out of the Egungun masquerade tradition.
3. Forms: tragedy (serious, ends in sorrow), comedy (light, ends happily), melodrama (exaggerated emotion, clear heroes and villains), farce (silly, fast, absurd situations), musical drama.
4. Elements: plot, character, theme, dialogue, setting, music and spectacle.
5. People: playwright, director, actors, producer, stage manager, designers (set, costume, lighting), prompter.

## Class activity

Groups read a short scene, decide whether it is tragedy or comedy, and list the elements and the people needed to put it on.

2. What is the difference between a tragedy and a comedy?
3. What does a stage manager do?

reading.title: Where drama comes from
reading.content:
# Drama and theatre

**Drama** is a story told by people who act it out in front of an audience. **Theatre** is the place and the art of presenting drama.

## How drama began

Drama began as part of **worship and community celebration**. People put on masks, danced, sang and acted to honour gods and ancestors and to remember their history.

- In ancient **Greece**, festivals honouring the god **Dionysus** grew into the first plays, the tragedies and comedies that are still studied today.
- In **Nigeria** and much of Africa, masquerade performances, such as the **Egungun** of the Yoruba, used costume, drumming, dance and story. The Yoruba **Alarinjo** travelling theatre grew from this tradition.
- The **Tiv** of central Nigeria have the **Kwagh-hir**, a performance with puppets, masks and songs that tells stories to the community.

## Forms of drama

- **Tragedy:** a serious story that ends in sorrow or disaster.
- **Comedy:** a light story that ends happily and makes people laugh.
- **Melodrama:** exaggerated emotion with clear heroes and villains.
- **Farce:** a fast, silly story with absurd situations.
- **Musical drama:** a play with songs and dances.

## Elements of drama

- **Plot:** the events, with a beginning, middle and end.
- **Characters:** the people in the story.
- **Theme:** the main idea or message.
- **Dialogue:** what the characters say.
- **Setting:** where and when the story takes place.
- **Music and sound.**
- **Spectacle:** what the audience sees, such as costumes and sets.

## The people who make a play

| Person | Job |
| --- | --- |
| Playwright | Writes the script |
| Director | Guides the actors and shapes the production |
| Actors | Play the characters |
| Producer | Finds the money and organises the production |
| Stage manager | Runs everything backstage during the show |
| Designers | Plan the costumes, set and lighting |
| Prompter | Helps an actor who forgets a line |

A play is the work of many people. The audience sees only the actors, but the show cannot happen without the rest.

reading.title: Behind the stage: the director
reading.content:
# The director

A play has a script, actors, costumes and lights. The **director** is the person who brings all of these together so that the audience sees one clear and moving story.

## The director's duties

1. **Study the script.** The director reads the play closely, decides what the main message is and how to show it.
2. **Cast the actors.** Through **auditions**, in which actors read or perform, the director chooses who plays each role.
3. **Plan the staging.** The director decides where actors stand and move. This is called **blocking**. Position tells the audience about the characters: a king may stand high and in the centre, a frightened servant lower and to the side.
4. **Rehearse.** The director leads rehearsals from the first reading to the full run-through, and coaches voice, movement and feeling.
5. **Give notes.** After a rehearsal, the director gives each actor **notes**, which are comments on what to change.
6. **Coordinate the designers.** The director works with the people who plan the set, the costumes, the lighting and the sound, so that they all serve one vision.
7. **Work with the stage manager.** The stage manager keeps the schedule and runs the show once it begins.
8. **Get the show ready.** The director makes sure everything is ready for opening night.

## Example: staging a scene

Scene: an angry king and a messenger who brings bad news.

- **Understand:** the king wants to punish someone; the messenger wants to survive.
- **Blocking:** the king stands upstage on a platform, in the centre. The messenger kneels downstage, to the side.
- **Movement:** as the king grows angrier he steps forward. The messenger backs away.
- **Voice:** the king speaks slowly and loudly. The messenger's voice is quick and shaky.
- **Rehearse:** run the scene many times, giving notes after each.

## Qualities of a good director

A good director listens, communicates clearly, plans carefully, stays calm under pressure and respects every person in the production.

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. state the functions of costume, makeup, lighting and set design;

4. The designers work from the director's idea and the script, and must keep actors safe.
5. Draw a ground plan for a small scene.

reading.content:
# Theatre design

When the curtain opens, the audience sees a world: clothes, colours, lights and a place. All of this is **design**. Designers work from the script and the director's idea.

## Costume and makeup

A **costume** tells the audience about a character. It can show:

- the character's **job or position**: a chief's robe, a nurse's uniform;
- **age and wealth**: rich cloth or old patched clothes;
- **time and place**: clothes of long ago or of today;
- **feelings**, through **colour**: red for anger or danger, white for purity, black for grief or evil.

Costumes must also be comfortable and safe so that the actor can move and speak freely. **Makeup** changes the face to suit the role: ageing, scars, or a bold design for a masquerade character.

## Lighting

Lighting does several jobs:

1. **Lets the audience see** the actors.
2. **Creates mood**: red light for danger or anger, soft blue for night or sadness.
3. **Shows time of day**: bright yellow-white for midday, orange for sunset.
4. **Focuses attention**: the audience looks at what is bright.

Terms to know:

- **Spotlight:** a lamp with a narrow, bright beam that lights one actor or one area.
- **Floodlight:** a lamp that lights a wide area softly.
- **Gel:** a thin sheet of coloured plastic in front of a lamp to change its colour.
- **Dimmer:** a control that raises or lowers the brightness.

## Set design

The **set** is the scenery that shows the place. A set designer plans it from the script and draws a **ground plan**.

- **Flats** are painted wooden or cloth frames that stand like walls.
- A **backdrop** is a large painted cloth hung at the back of the stage.
- **Props** (short for properties) are objects the actors use, such as a calabash, a walking stick or a stool.

A set may be **realistic**, looking like the real place, or **symbolic**, using a few shapes to suggest it, such as a single tree for a forest. A simple set is often better than a crowded one, because actors need room to move.

## Safety

Real fire is not safe on a stage. Use battery lamps for lanterns, and secure every piece of set so that nothing falls on an actor.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. explain improvisation and the rules that make it work;
2. improvise a short scene from a situation;

Situation cards (for example: two traders quarrel over a stall; a pupil arrives late and must explain), a copy of a short folktale, paper for scripts.

1. Improvisation is acting without a script: the actors make up the words and actions as they go.

5. Use the tortoise-and-birds folktale as a model: the invitation, the borrowed feathers, the feast, the fall.

## Class activity

Groups improvise one situation card, then plan and perform a three-scene dramatisation of the tortoise folktale using a narrator.

1. What is improvisation?
2. What should you do when your partner introduces a new idea?
3. What are stage directions?

reading.content:
# Improvisation and dramatising a story

## What is improvisation?

**Improvisation** is acting without a script. The actors make up the words and the actions on the spot, as the scene goes along. Improvisation trains actors to think fast, listen to each other and be confident.

## Rules of improvisation

1. **Agree on the basics:** who you are, where you are and what is happening.
2. **Accept and build.** If your partner says there is a snake in the room, react to it; do not say there is none. This is the "yes, and" rule.
3. **Listen** so that what you say fits what was just said.
4. **Stay in character** until the scene ends.
5. **Keep the scene going.** Do not stop to laugh or to argue.
6. **Support your partners.** A good improviser makes the other actor look good.

## Dramatising a story

To **dramatise** a story is to turn it into a play. You can dramatise a folktale, a poem or a chapter of a book.

1. **Choose the main events** and divide them into scenes.
2. **Assign the characters** and, if needed, a **narrator** who tells the audience what happens between scenes.
3. **Write short dialogue** for each scene. Keep it simple and let each character sound different.
4. **Add stage directions.** These are instructions, usually in brackets, about how a character moves or speaks: *(Tortoise flaps his arms like wings.)*
5. **Rehearse**, using voice and movement, and add simple costumes and props.

## Example: the tortoise and the birds

A folktale tells how the birds invite each other to a feast in the sky. The tortoise, who cannot fly, borrows a feather from each bird, gives himself the name "All of you" and, when the food is served for "all of you", eats everything himself. The angry birds take back their feathers, and the tortoise falls to earth and cracks his shell.

Scenes: 1. the invitation; 2. the borrowing of feathers; 3. the feast; 4. the fall.

## Using voice and movement

The tortoise can speak boastfully with a high, sly voice and move with small, clever steps. The birds fly with arms spread and speak sharply. A narrator speaks clearly and slowly to keep the story together.

reading.title: Making a living from drama
reading.content:
# Careers in drama

Drama is not only a school subject. It is a profession that supports thousands of Nigerians.

## Careers in the theatre and in film

| Career | What the person does |
| --- | --- |
| Actor | Plays a character on stage, film or television |
| Director | Guides the actors and the whole production |
| Playwright or scriptwriter | Writes the script |
| Producer | Finds the money and organises the production |
| Costume designer | Makes or chooses the clothes the characters wear |
| Set designer | Plans and builds the scenery |
| Makeup artist | Prepares the faces of the actors to suit their roles |
| Lighting and sound technician | Operates lights and sound |
| Cinematographer | Operates the camera and decides how scenes are filmed |
| Film editor | Cuts and joins the shots to make the final film |
| Stage manager | Runs everything backstage during a show |
| Casting director | Chooses actors for the roles |
| Theatre critic | Watches plays and writes what he or she thinks of them |
| Drama teacher | Trains learners in acting and stagecraft |

## Drama in Nigeria

Nigeria has a long tradition of stage drama, from the Yoruba travelling theatre to plays performed at university theatres and at the National Theatre in Lagos. Nigerian dramatists have written in English, Yoruba, Pidgin and other languages. Their plays often discuss politics, tradition and modern life, and some have won international attention.

Nigeria also has a huge film industry called **Nollywood**, which is among the largest in the world by the number of films made. Nollywood creates work for actors, camera crews, writers, makeup artists, caterers, drivers and many others, and its films show Nigerian life to audiences across Africa and the world.

## How drama helps society

1. It gives **jobs**.
2. It **entertains** and **preserves culture**: dress, food, music and languages.
3. It **educates**, by showing problems and moral lessons.
4. It **builds confidence and teamwork** in those who take part.

## Preparing for a career

- Join the school drama club and take part in productions.
- Read plays and watch good drama with attention.
